Data: [project details]
notes: Key message: a well-designed prompt can become a reusable template. Write it once, refine it, then use it every week. Steps 1 to 4 come from the original deck (step 4 included “refine the prompt”, now shown as step 5). Point out the techniques in the reusable prompt: - Role: “Act as a project coordinator”. - Audience: senior management. - Format: fixed sections, including a 3-line summary. - Grounding: “Base it only on the data below” (a simple form of RAG, preventing invented progress). - Safety net: “If anything is missing, list it under ‘Information needed’” instead of guessing. Encourage learners to keep a personal “prompt library”, a document of prompts that worked well, so they do not start from scratch each time.

text: Accountants: Categorising Expenses
Uses: drafting financial reports (balance sheets, income statements, tax summaries) from data, categorising expenses and spotting discrepancies, and explaining tax rules and possible deductions.
Workflow: expense categorisation
1. Prepare the data: collect the transactions and receipts to sort.
2. Write the prompt with the categories you want (right).
3. Input the list of expenses.
4. Review: check every category and fix mistakes.
5. Refine: ask for subcategories, such as Travel: flights, accommodation, meals.
PROMPT

Categorise the following expenses by type (Travel, Office Supplies, Client Entertainment, Utilities). Return a table with Date, Item, Amount and Category. Mark anything unclear as “Check”.
[list of expenses]
Always verify totals and tax advice with a qualified accountant and the current tax rules.
notes: Key message: accountants can use AI to speed up sorting, summarising and drafting, while keeping full responsibility for accuracy. The three uses and the 5-step workflow come from the original deck (the original split them across three slides). Point out the prompt techniques: - Fixed category list: the AI chooses only from your categories (like custom labels in classification). - Table format: easy to paste into a spreadsheet. - “Mark anything unclear as ‘Check’”: a safety net instead of guessing. Important cautions: - AI can make arithmetic mistakes. For totals, ask it to use code (the PAL technique) or check in a spreadsheet. - Tax rules change and differ by country. AI suggestions about deductions must be checked against current Ghana Revenue Authority rules or by a qualified professional. - Financial records are confidential. Remove names and account numbers, or use an approved company tool. Link to data labelling: categorising expenses is a labelling task. The same prompt pattern works for any categorisation job.

text: Researchers: Literature Reviews
Uses: summarising academic papers, finding trends and patterns in data, and structuring research proposals to fit a funder’s format.
Workflow: literature review
1. Collect papers relevant to your topic.
2. Write a summary prompt (right).
3. Provide the input: paste or upload the abstract or full text.
4. Review the summaries against the papers.
5. Ask for more detail, such as the theoretical framework or limitations.
PROMPT

Summarise the main findings, methodology and conclusions of the research paper below. Use headings for each. Quote the paper’s own words for key findings.
[paper text]
Never cite a paper you have not opened yourself. AI can invent references that look real.
notes: Key message: AI can save researchers many hours of reading and summarising, but every claim and every reference must be checked against the real source. The three uses and the 5-step workflow come from the original deck. Why the prompt asks for quotes: if the model must quote the paper’s own words for key findings, it is much easier to check that the summary is faithful, and harder for it to drift away from the source. The biggest risk is invented references, as learners saw in the hallucination hunt in the previous module. Rule: only cite what you have opened and read. Use the AI to summarise papers you supply (a form of RAG), not to find papers from memory, unless the tool searches real databases and gives links you then open. Data analysis: for statistics on real data, ask the AI to use code and show its working, and check the results.

text: Data Labelers: Prompting in Your Own Work
Prompt engineering is now part of many data labelling jobs, both using AI to help and evaluating what AI produces.
Understand the guidelines
“Explain this labelling rule in simple words and give me two examples of each label.”
Find tricky edge cases
“List 10 reviews that would be hard to label as positive or negative, and explain why.”
Write prompts and ideal answers
Many AI-training tasks ask you to write a prompt and a model answer, or to improve a weak one.
Rate and correct AI answers
Judge responses for accuracy, helpfulness and safety, then explain your rating. This is how chatbots get better.
notes: Key message: for data labelers, prompt engineering is not just a productivity trick; it is increasingly part of the job. This slide is an addition to the original deck, tailored to this training programme. Explain the four uses: - Understanding guidelines: AI can explain a confusing rule and generate examples. Always confirm with the official guideline or your team lead; the guideline is the authority, not the AI. - Edge cases: generating difficult examples helps you practise and helps teams improve guidelines. - Writing prompts and ideal answers: AI companies hire people to write prompts and high-quality “reference” responses that models learn from. Everything in this module, clear instructions, context, format and examples, applies directly. - Rating and correcting AI answers: this is called human feedback. Raters compare model answers, score them and explain why. It is one of the main ways chatbots are improved (reinforcement learning from human feedback, mentioned in the previous module). Important rule: never paste client data or confidential project material into public AI tools. Follow your project’s rules on AI use; some projects forbid it completely.

text: PRACTICAL 5 · CAPSTONE · 25 MIN · INDIVIDUAL
Build a Prompt for Your Own Work
Your task

Choose a real task from your work, studies or business.
Write a prompt using the template on the right.
Add one technique: examples, step-by-step or a review step.
Run it, review the answer and improve the prompt at least once.
Share your before-and-after prompt with a partner.
TEMPLATE

ROLE: Act as …
TASK: …
CONTEXT: This is for … because …
INPUT: [paste here]
FORMAT: Answer as …
LIMITS: Length, tone …
TECHNIQUE: [examples / think step by step / review]
If you are not sure, say so.
notes: This is the capstone of the module: learners apply everything to a task they actually care about. Give 15 minutes to build and test, then 10 minutes for partner sharing and a few volunteers presenting to the class. Suggest tasks if learners are stuck: writing a CV summary, planning a small business’s social media posts, preparing interview answers, summarising a long WhatsApp group discussion, drafting a complaint letter, creating a study plan, or writing labelling guidelines for a simple task. What to look for as you walk around: - Is the task a clear action verb? - Is there context the AI could not have guessed? - Is the format specified? - Did they add a technique and improve the prompt after the first run? Remind learners not to use real confidential information; invented or anonymised details are fine for practice. Encourage everyone to save their final prompt as the first entry in a personal prompt library.

text: Prompting Responsibly
Verify everything
Check facts, numbers, quotes and references. A good prompt reduces errors; it does not remove them.
Protect private data
Never paste personal, client or confidential information into public AI tools.
Watch for bias
Check whether answers treat people and groups fairly, and ask for balanced views.
Be open about AI use
Follow your school’s or employer’s rules, and say when AI helped with your work.
Keep learning yourself
Use AI to learn faster, not to stop thinking. Make sure you understand what you submit.
You are responsible
Whatever you send, publish or submit, you own it, not the AI.
notes: Key message: prompt engineering makes AI more useful, but responsibility for the result always stays with the person using it. Points to draw out: - Verify: links back to hallucinations. Even an excellent prompt can produce a wrong fact or an invented reference. - Private data: customer records, ID numbers, health information, passwords and confidential project material must not go into public chatbots. Many companies provide approved tools; some data labelling projects ban AI tools entirely. - Bias: ask for balanced perspectives and check whether examples or assumptions stereotype any group. - Transparency: the Nature extract in Part 3 was about researchers disclosing AI use. Schools and employers increasingly expect the same. - Keep learning: AI is a tutor and assistant, not a replacement for your own understanding. Discussion (3 minutes): “Which of these rules is easiest to forget in a busy day?”

text: Exit Quiz
Name the four elements of a prompt.
Rewrite “Write about malaria” as a specific prompt.
Why is it better to say what to do than what not to do?
What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
Which technique would you use for a multi-step maths problem, and what would you add to the prompt?
How does RAG help reduce hallucinations?
Give one reason to break a big task into a chain of prompts.
Name two things you should never paste into a public chatbot.
notes: Learners answer on paper individually (6 minutes), then swap and mark with a neighbour as you reveal the answers (4 minutes). Answers: 1. Instruction, context, input data, output indicator. 2. Any specific version with a clear task, audience, format and length, for example: “Explain how malaria spreads and three ways to prevent it, for parents in a rural community. Use simple English, a bulleted list, and under 150 words.” 3. Positive instructions give the model a clear path to follow. When a prompt only says what to avoid, the model may fall back on its usual pattern, which can be the very thing you wanted to avoid. 4. Zero-shot gives no examples; few-shot includes a handful of examples showing the task, format or style. 5. Chain-of-thought: add “Think step by step” or “Show your working”. Tools or code (PAL) are also acceptable. 6. It retrieves real information from documents, databases or search and gives it to the model, so the answer is based on real sources instead of the model’s memory. 7. Any one of: each step is simpler; you can check and correct each step before moving on; you get deeper answers to each part. 8. Any two of: personal data such as ID numbers, health records or passwords; client data; confidential company or project material; financial account details. Scoring: 6 or more correct means the learner is ready for intermediate prompt engineering. Fewer than 4: revisit the elements, the prompt formula and the cheat sheet.

text: KEY TAKEAWAYS
Four things to remember
A prompt is built from instruction, context, input data and output indicator.
Be specific: role, task, context, format and limits. Then test and improve.
Pick the technique for the problem: examples, step by step, chaining or sources.
You are responsible for what AI produces. Verify it and protect private data.
KEEP PRACTISING
Start a personal prompt library: save every prompt that works well, and improve it each time you use it.
notes: Close by reading the four takeaways. Ask each learner to share with a neighbour the one prompt from today they will actually use this week (1 minute). Homework: use the prompt formula on three real tasks this week. For each, write down the first prompt, the improved prompt, and what changed in the answer. Bring the best one to the next session. Next steps for interested learners: practise the core techniques (few-shot, chain-of-thought, chaining) until they are habits, then explore RAG and tool use in the AI products they use at work. Thank learners and collect feedback on the session.
